walkthroughs.body_html:
Principles of Chemistry — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Principles of Chemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Principles of Chemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition reactions?
options: Adding across a C=C would destroy the stable delocalised pi system; substitution preserves the aromatic ring.
Benzene contains three normal alternating double bonds and behaves like an alkene with three C=C.
Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.

mcqs.q: In 1H NMR, what does the n+1 rule predict?
options: Splitting tells you how many protons are in the same chemical environment as the one giving the peak.
A proton with n equivalent neighbouring protons will appear as a peak split into n+1 sub-peaks.
Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.
The number of peaks equals the total number of protons in the molecule.
